great-wave.description: A wave rears over three fishing boats like a hand of the sea, towering, its foam breaking into claw-like fingers, while far off Mount Fuji sits small and calm, still as a held breath. It is the opening gate of the series *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*. The print was made with the newly imported Prussian blue, a pigment carried in from beyond the sea. Thousands of impressions were made, and the wave has broken across the world ever since, until it has become perhaps the most famous Japanese artwork in the world.

saturn.description: A farmhouse outside Madrid. Its walls. The aged, deaf Goya painted straight onto them: 14 "Black Paintings", never meant for public view. This is one. The Titan Saturn, afraid his children will overthrow him. A headless body in his grip. He tears into it. His eyes wild with horror. In 1874 the murals came off the walls and were transferred to canvas. Now they are among the most disturbing images in the Prado. Never meant to be seen. Seen.

fallingwater.description: A house can face a waterfall, or it can stand on one. Fallingwater is a weekend house built directly over a waterfall for the Kaufmann family, its stacked concrete terraces cantilevered dramatically out over the falling water rather than facing it from a safe distance. Take that as the architecture's doctrine, and as yours: do not admire what moves you from the safe bank; step out over it. Widely considered Wright's masterpiece, it was designed when he was nearly 70, in the middle of what is often called his career's second, "Usonian" act. A second act can hold the masterpiece.

the-sick-child.description: I stand before a pale, red-haired girl propped on a pillow as she turns toward a grieving woman who bows her head beside the bed. I know the picture recalls the death of Munch's sister Sophie from tuberculosis. I see the scraping, the scratching, the repainting he gave the canvas for a year, until the surface seemed damaged. Critics mocked it as unfinished, but Munch called it a breakthrough, and he returned to the subject all his life. What grief is ever finished? I have scraped and repainted my own for years. Unfinished is not a flaw; it is the shape of mourning.

third-of-may.description: Stand in front of this painting and you stand at a threshold in how war is shown. It is the companion to *The Second of May*. At night, a faceless line of French soldiers aims its muskets at Spanish prisoners. At the centre a man in a white shirt flings his arms wide, lit by a lantern, his pose recalling the crucified Christ. Notice the architecture of it: the soldiers have no faces, and the light falls on the man before the muskets. It is one of the first great paintings to show war as senseless slaughter rather than glory, and it prepared the way for Manet and Picasso's *Guernica*. Once you see the men before the muskets as persons, glory is very hard to paint.

girl-with-a-pearl-earring.description: I was told this is not a portrait but a *tronie*, a study of a character or type, and still I want her name. A girl in an exotic blue and yellow turban turns over her shoulder toward me, lips parted, a large pearl gleaming at her ear. I lean in. I lean closer. I find the pearl is just two strokes of paint. How much of what I have loved was two strokes and my own longing? Often called the "Mona Lisa of the North", it inspired a best-selling novel and a 2003 film. I came for a girl and found a type, and I love her anyway.

genji-kashiwagi.description: Here is a scene from a later illustrated copy of the novel, drawn in monochrome ink line, the "hakubyō" manner, fine as frost traced on a winter pane. It belongs to a tradition distinct from the coloured Tokugawa and Gotoh scrolls also shown here, as a river by moonlight is distinct from the same river at noon. It stands as evidence of how continuously artists kept reinterpreting Murasaki's novel in new visual styles over the following centuries, each generation lowering its bucket into the same deep well.

sunflowers.description: Fifteen sunflowers stand in a yellow vase on a yellow table against a yellow wall, some bright and fresh as a summer morning, some wilting and going to seed like suns sinking at the end of their day. Van Gogh painted the canvas in Arles to decorate the room of his friend Paul Gauguin, as a host hangs banners in the hall for an honored guest. He made several versions, and the series became his signature: an exploration of how far one colour could go, a single light driven to the edge of the world, and a symbol of gratitude and friendship.

genji-yadorigi.description: A later chapter, painted in the same early 12th-century scroll tradition, where the light has passed on to the generation after Genji's death. His descendants navigate the same web of court rivalry, love and Buddhist renunciation that structures the novel's earlier chapters, a web spun long before them, its threads still catching the dew.

genji-sakaki.description: Another scene from the same monochrome hakubyō scroll, drawn in ink line alone, like a world seen by moonlight. It belongs to a genre of Genji illustration that favoured clarity of narrative detail over the saturated mineral colour of the earliest surviving scrolls, bare as winter branches where those were jewelled, and later painters often took it up as a study or reference copy, a map for their own journeys through the tale.

genji-suzumushi.description: A chapter named for the bell crickets set loose into a garden Genji has planted to evoke autumn, as if a season could be summoned by song. The scroll shows it with the restrained, geometric interior perspective and the stylised viewpoint of a roof blown away by the wind, the eye dropping like a bird into the rooms below, as is characteristic of this earliest surviving Genji scroll tradition.

genji-azumaya.description: Part of the novel's final "Uji chapters," where the tale drifts a generation past Genji's death and follows his descendants through romances tangled as vines. The scroll keeps faith with its own manner: the same muted mineral-pigment palette, the same roofless compositions seen from a bird's-eye height, as if the sky had lifted the lid from every house to look within.

masnavi-opening.description: Here the great river rises: the opening page of Rumi's six-book masterwork, some 25,000 couplets that flowed from him over the last decade or so of his life. They came at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, who wrote the verses down as Rumi recited them, catching each line as a cupped hand catches rain, reportedly even while the poet walked through the streets of Konya.

masnavi-peacock-parable.description: A doctrine is easier to carry when it arrives as a story. The Masnavi's six books hold hundreds of short parables and stories that Rumi wove through them to illustrate points of Sufi doctrine in accessible, often humorous form. Here is one: a peacock plucking out its own beautiful feathers to avoid the suffering its beauty attracts. The lesson is plain. It is a lesson on renouncing worldly vanity. Sometimes the ornament is the snare.

divan-e-shams.description: I stand before a vast collection of ecstatic lyric poems, tens of thousands of lines, and I think of the meeting that began them. Rumi composed them after meeting the wandering mystic Shams-e Tabrizi in 1244, an encounter that transformed him from a respected legal scholar into a poet. I read the title and it is not his own name. He named the entire collection after his friend and teacher rather than himself. Whose name would I sign on my own best work? Some meetings write the rest of a life.

fihi-ma-fihi.description: If you want to know how a teacher thinks, listen to the talk as well as the sermon. This is a collection of Rumi's informal talks and discourses to his disciples, recorded in prose rather than verse, covering everything from Quranic interpretation to everyday anecdotes. Scholars value it as the clearest direct record of how Rumi taught and argued outside the formal architecture of his poetry. Think of it as the workshop beside the cathedral. The verse is the monument; the talk is the doorway in.

sema-ceremony.description: Not a text but a living performance tradition, a river that has never stopped moving. It is associated with Rumi, and after his death his followers formalised it into the Mevlevi Sufi order: a turning dance performed to music and poetry, the dancers wheeling like slow stars, intended to induce a trance-like focus on the divine. The turning has not ceased. It continues to be performed at his shrine in Konya and by Mevlevi communities worldwide.

khusrau-matla-ul-anwar.description: The first of the five long narrative poems making up Khusrau's Khamsa (Quintet), the gate through which the whole procession enters. It was modelled on the Persian poet Nizami's own Khamsa, as a new tower rises in the shadow of an old one, but reworked with Khusrau's own didactic and mystical concerns. This folio illustrates one of its moral parables: a pilgrim humbled by an unexpected lesson in piety from a Hindu holy man.

khusrau-shirin-khusrau.description: What do you owe the voice that came before you? This is the second poem of the Khamsa, and it retells the romance of the Sasanian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shirin, a story Nizami had already told. The retelling was deliberate: an act of literary homage and rivalry, common practice among Persian poets responding to an admired predecessor's Khamsa. Notice the architecture of that lineage. To retell is to bow and to challenge in the same breath.

khusrau-majnun-layla.description: I stand before the third poem of the Khamsa, where Khusrau condensed the widely told Arabian legend of Layla and Majnun into his own tightly constructed Persian verse. I know these lovers. I know the families that drove them apart. I know the desert wilderness where Majnun wanders in grief-mad devotion. How much longing can a tight verse hold? More than I can. Love torn apart does not end; it wanders.

khusrau-hasht-bihisht.description: The fourth poem of the Khamsa, and a journey through colour. The Sasanian king Bahram Gur visits seven princesses, each housed in a differently coloured pavilion like a lamp burning with its own flame, and each telling him a story. The structure was adapted from Nizami's *Haft Paykar*, and it is often illustrated as a cycle of jewel-toned courtly scenes, glowing one after another like gems threaded on a string.

khusrau-aina-i-sikandari.description: The fifth and final poem of the Khamsa, where the quintet closes like a great gate. Here the legendary exploits of Alexander the Great are recast, and the conqueror becomes a philosopher-king. Khusrau drew partly on the same Alexander Romance tradition that stands behind Nizami's *Iskandarnama*, drinking from the old well, while adding battles and wonders of his own invention, new stars set in an old sky.

renunciation-of-worldly-goods.description: One of 28 scenes from the Legend of St Francis in Assisi, a saga told across walls. The young Francis strips off his clothes and hands them back to his furious father, while the bishop covers him with his cloak. The painting splits into two crowds, family on one side and Church on the other, and between them lies an empty gap, like the bare ground between two kingdoms. Scholars still argue over how much of the cycle is Giotto's own work, but its solid figures and clear storytelling point the road toward the Scrovegni Chapel.

scrovegni-chapel.description: The banker Enrico Scrovegni paid for this small chapel, and Giotto covered its whole interior with paint, wall upon wall, until the room became a book read by walking. Rows of scenes tell the lives of Joachim and Anna, the Virgin Mary and Christ, all beneath a deep blue vault scattered with gold stars, a night sky brought indoors. A Last Judgment fills the entrance wall. Below the stories, painted figures of the Virtues and Vices stand in grey, made to look like stone sculpture. It is the most complete surviving work by Giotto, and one of the great turning points in European art, a hinge on which the long door of painting swung.

kiss-of-judas.description: I stand before the kiss. Judas wraps Christ in a sweeping yellow cloak as he leans in for the kiss that betrays him. I see the two faces meet in profile, calm against treacherous. I see torches, clubs and lances crowding the sky above. I see, at the left, Peter cutting off a servant's ear. And still my eye returns to the faces. Giotto puts the whole drama into one locked gaze, which makes this one of the most psychologically charged images of the Middle Ages. Have I been kissed like that? Have I kissed like that? The closest betrayals come face to face.

lamentation.description: Mourners gather around the body of Christ, and I am among them. A bare, rocky ridge runs diagonally down the picture and leads my eye to his face, which Mary holds close to her own. Two figures sit with their backs to us, a bold idea that places me inside the circle of grief. I did not choose to sit down here. I was placed here. Above, angels twist and cry out in the sky. The fresco shows Giotto's gift for turning sacred stories into human feeling. Whose face have I held that close? Grief is a circle, and it always makes room for one more.

ognissanti-madonna.description: Painted for the church of Ognissanti in Florence, this huge altarpiece shows the Virgin enthroned among saints and angels. Now look at what changed. Earlier Madonnas, such as Cimabue's, look flat and weightless, like icons hung in air. Giotto's Virgin has real bulk: her knees push forward under her robe, and her throne recedes like a piece of architecture. That is the whole lesson in one body: the sacred is allowed to take up space. It hangs in the Uffizi beside the Madonnas of Cimabue and Duccio, so you can see the change for yourself. Weight, too, can be a kind of truth.

campanile.description: Some of what carries your name you will never see finished. In 1334 Florence appointed Giotto master of works for its cathedral, and he designed this bell tower beside it. He lived to see only the lowest storey built. Andrea Pisano and Francesco Talenti finished the tower in the 1350s, and still it carries his name. That is the covenant of architecture: one hand draws the threshold, others raise the walls, and the lineage keeps the first name. Its patterned facing of white, green and pink marble became one of the symbols of the city. Begin what you cannot finish; beginnings are remembered too.

ghent-altarpiece.description: A huge folding altarpiece, a heaven hinged in panels. When open, it shows God enthroned between Mary and John the Baptist, Adam and Eve at the far edges, and below them crowds of saints, prophets and pilgrims streaming across a flowering meadow like rivers running to the sea, all come to worship the Lamb of God. An inscription credits Jan's brother Hubert with beginning it and Jan with finishing it in 1432. It may be the most frequently stolen artwork in history. One panel, the *Just Judges*, taken in 1934, has never been found; its place in the constellation stays dark.

man-in-a-turban.description: A sharply lit face turns out of a black background, framed by a red headdress folded in astonishing detail. I meet its steady sideways gaze and I do not look away. The original frame carries van Eyck's motto *Als ich can* ("As I can") and the date 21 October 1433. As I can. I say it under my breath: as I can, as I can. That gaze has led many to believe this is a self-portrait, perhaps painted with the help of a mirror. What would I see if I painted myself as I can, and not as I wish? Doing what you can, with care, is its own honesty.

arnolfini-portrait.description: I stand at the edge of a room in Bruges. An Italian merchant, probably Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, stands hand in hand with a woman in a green gown. On the back wall a convex mirror reflects the couple from behind, along with two more figures in the doorway. Above it, van Eyck signed in elegant script: "Jan van Eyck was here 1434". I read it twice. Was here. Every object is painted with microscopic care, and I count them: the brass chandelier, the oranges on the windowsill, the little dog. The picture has invited endless theories about marriage, memory and symbolism, and I bring no theory, only this: every careful picture says I was here.

madonna-of-chancellor-rolin.description: Nicolas Rolin, the powerful chancellor of Burgundy, kneels in prayer across from the Virgin and Child, as an angel lowers a crown onto Mary's head. Behind them, three arches open like windows onto another realm: a river valley painted in miniature, a bridge, a city, boats and tiny people, all fading into blue distance as a dream fades at dawn. That landscape shows van Eyck's mastery of detail at every scale, from a crown within reach to a city at the edge of sight.

madonna-van-der-paele.description: Precision is a form of attention. The elderly canon Joris van der Paele, spectacles in hand, is presented to the Virgin by St George, while St Donatian stands at the left. Look closely and you will see the method: van Eyck painted the old man's wrinkled skin, the shining armour and a richly patterned oriental carpet with such precision that they seem almost real enough to touch. The painting is a showcase of what oil paint could do, a demonstration of the medium's whole grammar. Attention, given fully, brings the distant within reach.

margaret-van-eyck.description: The artist's wife, then 33, looks directly out at us, and I feel her looking at me. This is among the earliest European portraits of an artist's spouse. Its original frame records that "my husband Johannes completed me" on 17 June 1439. Completed me. I turn the words over in my hands. The painting is plain and unflattering, but warm: a record of a real person rather than an ideal. Who would paint me as I am? Would I let them? To be seen plainly and kindly is the rarest gift.

four-seasons-autumn.description: One of a set of four tall scrolls, the seasons turning like a great wheel, painted in the monumental style of Chinese landscape painting: towering cliffs, a temple half hidden in trees, houses in a misty valley where the air hangs like breath. Works like this show how carefully Sesshū studied the Chinese masters of the Song and Ming dynasties, before and during his journey to China, as a traveller learns the stars before setting out and keeps reading them on the road.

autumn-and-winter-landscapes.description: Two small scrolls that are among the most admired works of Japanese ink painting. In *Winter*, a single jagged black line plunges down through the sky beside a cliff like a crack running through the world. It is not really a mountain edge, and it slices the composition in two with startling abstract force. Below, a lone traveller climbs toward a temple through the snow, a snow suggested only by blank paper, white as silence.

haboku-landscape.description: What does it mean to pass on a craft? Painted for his disciple Josui Sōen as a certificate of his training, this landscape is made almost entirely of wet, splashed washes of ink. Now watch: a few quick dark strokes turn the blots into a wine-shop flag, a roof, a boat and two tiny figures. Above it Sesshū wrote a long inscription about his teachers and his trip to China, a genealogy set down beside the gift. It is a celebrated example of the spontaneous "broken ink" style. Mastery is the moment chaos accepts a few right strokes.

huike-offering-his-arm.description:
Painted when Sesshū was 76. A Zen legend. The monk Huike, refused as a disciple by Bodhidharma. So he cuts off his own arm. To prove his sincerity. Bodhidharma sits meditating before a cave wall. A heavy, unbroken outline. Unmoved. Huike stands beside him, holding his severed arm. Around them the rock swirls. The simple figure does not. That bold contrast makes it one of the great images of Zen art.

Still unmoved.

flowers-and-birds.description: Decoration is also a way of keeping time. Pines, plum trees, water and birds stretch across large folding screens, moving through the year from spring to winter, so that a single room holds the whole turning year. Screens like these, painted in Sesshū's manner, helped make bird-and-flower painting a staple of Japanese interior decoration, part of the very architecture of a room. They prepared the way for the grand screens of the Kanō school. What you hang on your walls can become a lineage.

view-of-ama-no-hashidate.description: One of Sesshū's last works, and one of the earliest large views of a real Japanese place. The famous pine-covered sandbar of Ama-no-Hashidate stretches across the bay like a green thread drawn over the water, surrounded by temples, shrines and villages, many labelled with their names as on the map of a known realm. Painted in his eighties, it shows the old master turning from Chinese models to the scenery of his own country, the long road of his art arriving at its own doorstep.

lofty-mount-lu.description: A towering mountain of stacked peaks, waterfalls and pines rises like a stair into the sky, with a tiny scholar standing at its foot. Shen Zhou painted it as a 70th-birthday gift for his teacher Chen Kuan. The mountain's grandeur is a tribute to the old man's character, virtue lifted into stone. He had never visited Mount Lu. He painted it in the dense, textured manner of the Yuan master Wang Meng, and it is one of his largest and most ambitious works.

boating-on-an-autumn-river.description: I watch a small boat drift on a quiet river beneath autumn trees and distant hills. The tall, narrow format leads my eye upward through the landscape, and I let it lead me. Scenes of boating, visiting friends and retreat were favourite themes of the Suzhou literati, who valued leisure and friendship above official careers. I think of my own ledger of hours. When did I last choose a friend over a deadline? When did I last drift? A life is measured by its unhurried hours.

walking-with-a-staff.description: A small scholar with a walking stick pauses among tall, slender trees near a stream and a thatched pavilion, beneath towering, rounded mountains that stand like old guardians. The dry ink and clean contours follow the Yuan painter Ni Zan, whose austere style Shen Zhou admired but found hard to imitate, as clear spring water is hard to carry in the hand. Here he makes it fuller and bolder. The figure is often read as a self-portrait of the artist, a wanderer set within his own world.

night-vigil.description: Shen Zhou sits awake in a small house among mountains late at night. Above the painting he wrote a long essay describing how, in the silence, he listened to the sounds of the night: wind, dogs, a distant drum. The experience cleared his mind. I read it and I remember my own nights. I remember the wind. I remember a dog somewhere down the road. I remember the drum of my own pulse when sleep would not come. Text and image together make this a rare, intimate record of a Chinese painter's inner life. Why does the dark teach us to listen? Silence is where the mind is swept clean.

poet-on-a-mountaintop.description: A scholar stands alone on a clifftop, gazing across an empty valley veiled in mist, like one who has reached the rim of the world. Shen Zhou's poem, written into the sky itself, imagines the white clouds like a sash wound around the mountains. The vast empty space, the simple forms and the fusion of painting, poetry and calligraphy, three streams meeting in one still pool, make this small album leaf one of the most loved images in Chinese art.

crabs.description: Greatness does not live only in the grand. Three crabs clamber among reeds at the water's edge, each drawn with a few wet, confident strokes of ink, and a short poem in Shen Zhou's hand is written above them. He enjoyed painting everyday subjects such as vegetables, fruit, birds, cats and crabs, which were a favourite autumn delicacy in Suzhou. These quick, humorous sketches show the lively side of an artist better known for grand landscapes. Think of it as the other half of the ledger: the mountain and the supper. A whole life keeps room for both.

seven-deadly-sins.description: A painted tabletop. Arranged like a giant eye. At its centre, inside the "pupil", Christ rises from his tomb above the Latin warning *Beware, beware, the Lord sees*. Around him, seven scenes of everyday life act out the sins. Gluttony. Sloth. Lust. Pride. Anger. Envy. Avarice. Four roundels in the corners. Death. Judgment. Heaven. Hell. Philip II of Spain kept it in his bedroom at the Escorial. Some scholars now credit it to Bosch's workshop or a follower. Whoever's hand it was, the eye is open.

ship-of-fools.description: A leaky boat. Drifting nowhere. Its crew: a monk, a nun, a crowd of drunken revellers. They sing. They gorge. They snap at a dangling cake. A tree serves as the mast. In its branches, a jester perches. It is a fragment of a larger triptych, and it mocks human folly and corrupt clergy with the sharp humour of its day. Still leaking. Still drifting. Still nowhere.

temptation-of-st-anthony.description:
The desert hermit Anthony kneels in prayer. Around him, chaos swirls. Fish that fly like airships. Demons in armour. A black mass in a ruined tower. A city burning on the horizon. Bosch invented a whole world of hybrid monsters to show the saint's inner struggle against temptation. He kneels. It swirls. The painting inspired later Surrealists.

The monsters kept breeding.

garden-of-earthly-delights.description: Bosch's most famous and mysterious work, a world told in three panels like a saga that runs from dawn to ruin. The left panel shows God presenting Eve to Adam in Paradise. The huge centre panel teems with naked figures frolicking among giant birds, strawberries and crystal fountains, a summer without a horizon. The right panel is a nightmarish, frozen Hell of musical torture instruments and the "Tree-Man". Whether it is a warning against sin or a vision of a lost innocence, scholars still disagree after five centuries, and the garden keeps its secret like a sealed spring.

haywain-triptych.description: Look at what people will fight for. A giant cart of hay, a Flemish symbol of worthless worldly goods, rolls toward Hell pulled by demons. People of every class, from pope and emperor down, grab at the hay or fight and kill each other to get it. On top, a pair of lovers ignore the angel praying beside them. The story reads left to right, from the Fall in Eden to damnation, a ledger kept in paint. Read it as a doctrine of appetite: the cart keeps rolling while you grab. What you clutch at is also what carries you.

christ-carrying-the-cross.description: No landscape. No sky. Only faces. A tight crush of grotesque, jeering faces, pressed around the calm, closed-eyed Christ. Closer. Closer. Saint Veronica, holding the cloth with his image, turns away in the corner. The composition is claustrophobic and almost modern. Its attribution to Bosch himself is debated. The faces stay.

dancing-dervishes.description: I stand among the ones who look on. Sufi mystics whirl and leap in ecstatic dance in a flowering garden while others watch, some calm, some overcome with emotion. Which of them am I? Every figure has a distinct pose and expression, and I search the page for mine. The painting captures the *sama*, the Sufi ceremony of music and movement, with a liveliness that marks the new naturalism of the Herat school. I remember being moved and not knowing why. Some of us dance and some of us are undone, and both are a way of standing near the holy.

timur-granting-audience.description: From an illustrated history of the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane), made for Sultan Husayn Bayqara. Timur sits enthroned beneath a canopy at his accession in 1370, like a sun at the centre of its turning court, while courtiers and guards fill a flowering garden in a crowded yet ordered composition. This is one half of a double-page scene attributed to the young Behzād. It shows the courtly world he would record throughout his career, the first page of a long chronicle of gardens and gold.

seduction-of-yusuf.description: Resistance has an architecture. In Behzād's most famous painting, the story of Yusuf (Joseph) and Zulaikha (Potiphar's wife) is set in a fantastic palace of staircases, doorways and tiled rooms. Zulaikha has led Yusuf through seven locked chambers, but as she reaches for him, the doors fly open and he escapes. See how the building does the teaching: the maze-like architecture becomes an image of the soul resisting desire. The signed work is one of the high points of Persian painting. Every locked door is also a threshold out.

construction-of-khawarnaq.description: Instead of a royal scene, Behzād painted the hands that raise a palace: labourers carry bricks up ladders rung by rung, masons lay courses, a man mixes mortar, another hauls water. Each figure is individually observed, each bent to a different task, as every star keeps its own place in a constellation. It is one of the most celebrated images of labour in Islamic art, and it shows Behzād's interest in the everyday world, the ground on which every throne is built.

alexander-and-the-hermit.description: Power has to dismount sometimes. The world conqueror Iskandar (Alexander the Great) dismounts to visit a wise hermit living in a cave in a wild, rocky landscape. It is a lesson in humility before spiritual wisdom, and you can read it in the movement itself: the one who rules the world comes down to the one who lives in a cave. Alexander may be given the features of Behzād's patron, Sultan Husayn Bayqara, and the gnarled trees and rocks show the Herat school's delight in nature. The higher you ride, the farther you must step down.

sultan-husayn-bayqara.description: I look at the last great Timurid ruler of Herat, Behzād's patron, sitting cross-legged in a plain robe. I expected a king. I find a man. His face is shown as that of a specific, ageing man rather than an idealised king. The painting is a copy after Behzād's lost original, a face outliving its first likeness. Such individual portraits were a new development in Persian painting, and they influenced portraiture at the Mughal and Ottoman courts. Who will remember my face as it was, and not as I wished it? Even a copy can keep a person true.

annunciation.description: Beginnings are allowed to be imperfect. Probably painted while Leonardo was still in Verrocchio's workshop, this is one of his earliest surviving paintings. The angel Gabriel kneels on a flowering lawn to greet the Virgin. The angel's wings were modelled on a real bird's, and a hazy landscape of trees and mountains opens up behind. There are youthful mistakes in the perspective. But look at the careful study of nature, because it points to everything that came later. Your early errors are not your prophecy; your early attention is.

virgin-of-the-rocks.description: Mary, the infant Jesus, the infant John the Baptist and an angel sit in a shadowy grotto of strange rock formations and carefully observed plants, gathered as if in the hollow of the earth's own hand. Leonardo bound the figures together with glances and gestures in a pyramid shape, and modelled them with soft shadow, the technique later called *sfumato*, where light melts into dark like evening mist over water. A second version, painted after a dispute with the patrons, hangs in the National Gallery, London, a twin born of a quarrel.

lady-with-an-ermine.description: Cecilia Gallerani, the teenage companion of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, turns as if someone had just called to her, and I almost answer. She holds a sleek white ermine, a pun on her surname and a symbol of the duke. I watch the twisting pose. I watch her long, expressive hand. I watch a turn that is never finished. That pose and that hand brought a new sense of life and movement to the Italian portrait. Who is calling me, and do I turn? Life in a picture is the moment just before the answer.

vitruvian-man.description: Architecture begins with the body. A man with arms and legs in two positions fits inside both a circle and a square, illustrating the Roman architect Vitruvius's claim that the ideal human body mirrors the geometry of the universe. Leonardo's notes in mirror-writing record the proportions he measured. Because it is fragile and light-sensitive, the drawing is rarely displayed. Even so, it has become a universal symbol of the union of art and science. Sit with that: the sheet stays in the dark while its image goes everywhere. A symbol can travel farther than the paper it lives on.

last-supper.description: Painted on the refectory wall of a Milanese convent, it holds the moment Christ announces that one of his disciples will betray him. The apostles recoil in waves of shock and questioning, like water struck by a stone, grouped in threes. All the lines of the architecture lead to Christ's head, as the spokes of a wheel run to its hub. Leonardo experimented with painting on dry plaster so that he could work slowly, but the paint began flaking within his lifetime, the wall shedding its vision like leaves in autumn. A 21-year restoration ended in 1999.

mona-lisa.description: Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, sits before a dreamlike landscape that recedes like memory, her smile hovering at the edges of her mouth and eyes like light on the skin of a pool. Leonardo kept the portrait for the rest of his life and reworked it for years, blurring its transitions with *sfumato*, as mist softens the seam between hill and sky. Its theft from the Louvre in 1911, and its return two years later, helped make it the most famous painting in the world: the lost thing found, and never again unknown.

self-portrait-1500.description: Dürer faces us head-on, in the symmetrical pose normally used for images of Christ, and I cannot look away. His hair falls in perfect ringlets. His hand touches the fur of his coat. The Latin inscription states that he painted himself "in everlasting colours" at age 28. I remember wanting to be seen. I remember not daring to say so. I remember how long I waited for permission. It is a daring claim for the dignity of the artist, whose creative gift was seen as a reflection of God's. What would I dare to claim for my own gift? To make something is to stand, a little, in the maker's light.

young-hare.description: I lean in toward a crouching hare, painted fur by fur, its ears alert and whiskers catching the light. A window is reflected in its eye, and I almost look for myself there. Dürer's nature studies were far ahead of their time. This one shows an animal as an individual living creature, not a symbol. Not a symbol. A someone. It became one of the most copied images in German art. How often have I looked at a living thing and seen only what it stood for? To be seen as yourself is the first tenderness.

adam-and-eve.description: Dürer's showpiece of the ideal human body, drawn from classical proportions he had studied in Italy. Adam and Eve stand in a dark forest full of animals, like the first dawn caught at the edge of the first night, and each animal stands for one of the four medieval "temperaments". A small tablet hanging from a branch carries his proud signature, a banner hung in the first garden. The engraving's range of tones, from bright skin to velvety black, shows his total command of the burin, a blade that could summon both day and night.

knight-death-and-the-devil.description: A gloomy ravine. An armoured knight rides through it. Steady. Death holds up an hourglass. The knight ignores him. A pig-snouted devil lurks behind. Ignored too. It is one of Dürer's three "Master Engravings". It is often read as an image of the Christian who keeps to the path of faith despite fear and temptation. The sand keeps running. He keeps riding.

melencolia-i.description:
A winged figure. Brooding. Around her, scattered tools of measurement and craft. A compass. A polyhedron. A sphere. An hourglass. Behind her hangs a magic square. Its rows add up to 34. Its bottom row contains the year: 1514. It has been called the most debated print ever made. It is often read as a portrait of the creative mind stalled by doubt.

Stalled. Still stalled.

rhinoceros.description: In 1515 an Indian rhinoceros arrived in Lisbon, the first seen in Europe since Roman times, a wonder carried from far shores. Dürer never saw it. He worked from a letter and a sketch, and imagined an animal clad in riveted armour plates, like a knight forged by some smith of the wild, with a small extra horn on its back. The print sold in thousands and remained Europe's standard picture of a rhinoceros for about 250 years, a creature of rumour standing in for the truth.

pieta.description: I stand before a mother holding her dead son across her lap. Michelangelo made it in his early twenties, for a French cardinal's tomb: the Virgin cradling the dead Christ. Her calm, youthful face. The heavy folds of her robe. The marble turned to flesh and cloth. I have seen grief look older than this. Why is hers so calm? It is the only work he ever signed: his name is carved on the sash across Mary's chest. Vasari says he added it after hearing visitors credit the statue to another sculptor. I understand wanting to be known for what you made. But I keep looking at her face, not his name. Some sorrow runs so deep it looks like peace.

david.description: Carved from a tall, narrow block that other sculptors had abandoned, this giant David is shown before his fight with Goliath, tense, watchful and fully alert, like a drawn bowstring in the breath before release. The Florentine Republic set it in front of the Palazzo Vecchio as a symbol of the city's defiance of stronger enemies, a vow carved in stone. It was moved indoors in 1873, and a copy now stands in its original place, a sentinel's twin keeping the old watch.

doni-tondo.description: I stand before Michelangelo's only generally accepted finished panel painting, made for the wedding of the merchant Agnolo Doni. Mary, Joseph and the Christ Child twist together in a tight spiral of sculptural bodies and sharp, acid colours. I know that knot. I know how a family can hold on and pull at once. I know how close is never quite still. Nude youths lounge in the background, apart from it all. The original carved frame, probably designed by Michelangelo himself, survives, a circle around the circle. What holds a family, if not the frame we build around it? Love is a spiral, not a line.

creation-of-adam.description: The best-known scene of the vast Sistine ceiling, which Michelangelo painted largely by himself for Pope Julius II. God, borne on a swirl of angels like a storm cloud full of wings, reaches toward the languid Adam; their fingers almost, but not quite, touch, and in that narrow gap all of creation holds its breath. Around this and eight other Genesis scenes, he painted prophets, sibyls, ancestors of Christ and 20 muscular nudes, over 300 figures in all, a heaven crowded with the living.

moses.description: The centrepiece of the tomb of Julius II, a project that dragged on for 40 years like a winter that would not break, and that Michelangelo called "the tragedy of the tomb". The seated prophet grips the tablets of the law, his beard flowing like water, his gaze fierce as a desert wind. The horns on his head come from a traditional mistranslation of the Hebrew for "rays of light": light, in the retelling, hardened into horn.

last-judgment.description:
More than 20 years after the ceiling, Michelangelo came back. The altar wall. He covered it with a whirling vision of the end of time. A powerful, beardless Christ raises his arm. The saved rise. The damned are dragged down. Its crowds of nudes caused scandal, and after the Council of Trent another painter was hired to add draperies. Then St Bartholomew. He holds a flayed skin. Its face is thought to be Michelangelo's self-portrait.

His own face. Emptied. Held in another's hand.

sehzade-mosque.description: Every master keeps an apprenticeship, even after the title arrives. Built for Suleiman the Magnificent in memory of his son Şehzade Mehmed, who died young, this was Sinan's first major imperial commission after his appointment as chief architect. He later called it his "apprenticeship work," and the plan shows it: here he experimented with a four-semi-dome plan around a central dome, a grammar he would refine for the rest of his career. Its twin minarets each carry two balconies. Notice the architecture of a life's work: a memorial and a lesson at once. Your first real attempt is allowed to be a school.

suleymaniye-mosque.description: Architecture can be a covenant with a whole city. This is the centrepiece of a vast charitable complex built for Suleiman the Magnificent, with hospitals, schools, a soup kitchen, baths and a caravanserai gathered around the mosque itself. Think of it as prayer with its sleeves rolled up. Sinan called it his "journeyman work," a step toward surpassing the ancient dome of Hagia Sophia nearby; even at this scale, he counted himself on the way. Sinan and Suleiman are both buried in domed mausoleums in its garden, builder and patron in the same ledger of stone. Where you rest says what you served.

selimiye-mosque.description: Some goals take a lifetime, and that is not failure; it is the shape of devotion. Built for Selim II in the former Ottoman capital of Edirne, this is the building Sinan himself called his masterpiece, completed at about eighty years old. Eight massive piers carry a dome whose diameter finally exceeded that of Hagia Sophia, the target he had chased his whole career, while four slender, fluted minarets frame the courtyard. Picture it: a working life measured against one dome, and the answer arriving at the end. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Keep chasing your dome; the architecture of a life is finished last.

rustem-pasha-mosque.description: A small mosque for grand vizier Rüstem Pasha, raised on a shopping arcade above a busy market street. Its modest footprint hides an interior sheathed almost floor to ceiling in high-quality İznik tile, in the tomato-red that marks the finest production of the period, more densely tiled than any other Ottoman mosque of its size. Here is the lesson in plain terms: the threshold can be humble while the room within is a treasury. You rise from the noise of the market into a covenant of colour. Never judge a life by its footprint.

mihrimah-sultan-mosque.description: Built at the city's highest point for Mihrimah Sultan, Suleiman the Magnificent's daughter, on a hilltop site that let Sinan ring the single dome with an exceptional number of windows, so that light floods the prayer hall like a spring filling a basin. A popular, likely apocryphal legend reads the light effects at the spring and autumn equinoxes as a tribute to her name, which means "sun and moon." True or not, the tale clings to the hilltop as the light does, a crown of brightness on the city's brow.

villa-rotonda.description: A good design answers its site. This country retreat for a retired papal official was built on a hilltop with views in every direction, and it was answered with a design of near-perfect symmetry: four identical temple-fronted porticoes, one on each face, around a central domed rotunda. Every direction is given a front; no view is made the back. Left unfinished at Palladio's death, it was completed by his pupil Vincenzo Scamozzi and became the most copied private house plan in Western architecture. That is lineage in its purest form: the student finishes the sentence, and the world keeps repeating it.

basilica-palladiana.description: Renewal sometimes means wrapping the old rather than tearing it down. This was Palladio's first major public commission and the building that made his reputation: a new classical skin wrapped around Vicenza's crumbling medieval town hall. His solution, a two-storey arcade of round arches framed by smaller flanking openings, a motif now called the Palladian window, let the load-bearing masonry flex slightly without cracking the stonework. Read that as a doctrine: good architecture leaves room to move. Construction continued for decades after his death. What bends a little does not have to break.

teatro-olimpico.description: Every architecture of illusion begins as an architecture of study. This was Palladio's last design, a covered theatre modelled on his study of ancient Roman precedent, and he did not live to see it done: Scamozzi completed it after his death. Now look behind the stage arch. Streets built in forced perspective recede at a scale that makes them appear far longer than the shallow space allows. Said plainly, a shallow stage, disciplined by perspective, can hold whole streets. The illusion is still in use here, at the world's oldest surviving indoor theatre in continuous use. Some thresholds are deeper than the rooms behind them.

san-giorgio-maggiore.description: Every building carries an awkward truth; the art is in how gracefully it is carried. Here is a monastery church on its own island, across the water from St Mark's Square. A basilica's profile is awkward: a tall nave, lower side aisles. Palladio's answer was a bright white facade in which two classical temple fronts of different heights overlap to mask that profile. The facade is a grammar of concealment that reads as candour. It was a problem he solved more elegantly here than any architect before him. Elegance is a difficulty that has been listened to.

il-redentore.description: Some buildings are promises kept in stone. This votive church was commissioned by the Venetian Senate after a plague that killed roughly a third of the city's population, and the covenant has not lapsed: every July it is still visited in a procession of thanksgiving, carried across the water on a footbridge. Step inside to meet the vow's quieter side. Its luminous white facade and centrally planned interior, lit from hidden windows, are considered among the calmest and most resolved of all Palladio's church designs. After loss a city asked for a building; the building answered with calm. Gratitude, too, needs an architecture.

netherlandish-proverbs.description: Here was a village where speech had put on flesh. More than 100 sayings walked its lanes, each one taken literally, as if the proverbs of the land had been loosed like starlings and had settled into bodies. A man banged his head against a brick wall. Another filled in the well after the calf had drowned. A woman tied the devil to a pillow. The painting is both a comic encyclopedia of folly, a codex of every foolishness the tongue has named, and a portrait of a world turned upside down, its sky spilled at its feet like water from an upended bowl.

childrens-games.description:
I count some 230 children, about 80 games, and I lose count, as I did as a child. Leapfrog, hoops, stilts. Blind man's buff, spinning tops. Children playing at weddings, children playing at processions, filling a whole town square. From above, as the painting shows them, they are a remarkable record of 16th-century play.

I remember the rules we swore by. I remember how gravely we played at being grown. Is this a record, or a mirror? It may also carry a moral: that adult affairs are just as foolish as a child's games. We never stop playing; we only stop admitting it.

tower-of-babel.description:
A tower. Colossal. Spiralling up above a Flemish harbour city, modelled on Rome's Colosseum. In the foreground King Nimrod inspects the work. Around him, hundreds of tiny labourers. Hauling stone. Working the cranes. Building scaffolding, level on level.

Look again. The tower is already leaning. The lower levels are crumbling. The top is not yet finished, and the bottom is already coming apart. A warning about human pride.

And still they haul the stone.

hunters-in-the-snow.description: Three tired hunters came home over the hill with their dogs at their heels, and the whole harvest of their day was a single fox. Below them the valley lay locked in winter under a green-grey sky, pale as old ice over deep water, and on the frozen ponds the villagers skated, small and dark as seeds scattered across snow. The panel belongs to a series of six paintings of the seasons, made for the Antwerp merchant Nicolaes Jonghelinck, a wheel of the year turned in oil. Of all the winters that art has kept, this is one of the most beloved.

the-harvesters.description: Another of the seasons series, and here the year stood in late summer, heavy and gold. Peasants scythed the golden wheat and bound it into bundles, their blades flashing like light on water. Others rested beneath a pear tree to eat bread, porridge and cheese, and one lay sprawled asleep, as if the heat had pressed him into the earth. Beyond them the land ran on to a hazy bay. No god descends here, and no hero rides through. It is one of the first great paintings of ordinary working life, with no religious or mythological story attached: only the field, the meal and the long light.

peasant-wedding.description: In a barn the feast was laid, and the food came in on a door. Two men carried bowls of porridge upon it, the door lifted from its hinges for the feast, while a piper watched the food with hungry eyes and a child licked a plate as clean as a moon. The bride sat beneath a paper crown before a green cloth, still as a lantern amid the din. Which guest is the groom is still debated, a riddle the painting keeps. Every corner brims with affectionate, comic detail, and the painting is one of the reasons for Bruegel's nickname, "Peasant Bruegel".

the-chess-game.description:
Three of Sofonisba's sisters, Lucia, Minerva and Europa, play chess outdoors while a servant looks on, and I find myself counting my own. Lucia has just made the winning move, and she glances out at us. Minerva raises a hand in protest. Little Europa grins.

I remember the table. I remember the protest. I remember the grin. Chess was a game of intellect, so the painting quietly shows off the family's education. Is that pride, or love, or both? It brings unusual warmth and spontaneity to a group portrait. We are shaped by what we learn, and by who we learn it beside.

self-portrait-at-the-easel.description: She looks straight at me, brush in hand, and I am the one who looks away first. Anguissola paints herself at work on an image of the Virgin and Child. At a time when women were rarely allowed to train as artists, the self-portrait is a statement of her professional identity. I read it as a triad: the work, the hand, the name. She painted more self-portraits than any other artist between Dürer and Rembrandt. How many times must you say who you are before the world writes it down? Some of us have to paint ourselves into the record.

family-portrait.description: A father sits before a landscape with his only son, Asdrubale, and his daughter Minerva, and I think of my own father's hands. The boy clutches a small dog. The relaxed, affectionate poses were unusual for a formal family portrait, and I feel it before I can name it. This is the artist's father. Amilcare had championed his daughters' education. He sent Sofonisba's work to Michelangelo. What is love, if not sending someone's work out ahead of them? Some love is a door held open.

bernardino-campi.description: Here is a double portrait with a twist, a mirror set within a mirror. Sofonisba showed her teacher, Bernardino Campi, at work upon her portrait, yet it was her hand that painted the whole picture, teacher and all. Her own likeness she made larger and brighter than the one taking shape beneath his hand, a lamp outshining the lamp that first lit it. It is a witty meditation on authorship, on teaching, and on who holds the brush.

elisabeth-of-valois.description: I see the gown first: black, embroidered with gold, every jewel rendered in minute detail, as the formal conventions of the Spanish court required. I see the miniature next, her husband, Philip II, held small in her hand. Only then do I see the tenderness. She is the young French-born Queen of Spain, and she was Anguissola's pupil and friend. The portrait carries a personal tenderness born of the two women's years together. I remember a friend who taught me. What can a convention hold, if not the warmth beneath it? Love can wear black and gold and still be love.

philip-ii.description: The king holds a rosary, in sober black with the Order of the Golden Fleece, and I look past him for the hand that painted him. For centuries this portrait was credited to the court painter Alonso Sánchez Coello. For centuries her name was missing. Modern research returned it to Anguissola, one of several of her court works that had lost her name. How many names have slipped from the things we made? A name returned is not a gift; it is a debt repaid.

origin-of-music.description: It comes from one of the earliest manuscripts made for the young emperor Akbar: a collection of tales told by a wise parrot, one story threaded after another like beads on a silk cord. This page, attributed to Basawan, illustrates a story about how music was first discovered, the hour a silent world first learned to sing. Already its figures are lively and its colours bright, the marks of the new Mughal style, where Persian and Indian painting met and mingled like two rivers joining.

drunk-european.description: A man in European dress sat slumped on the ground with a wine flask, and shadow had been laid upon him with care, so that he swelled from the page with weight and volume. Strangers had come to the court: Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries had lately arrived at Akbar's court, bearing European prints and paintings like seeds blown from a far country. Basawan was among the first Mughal artists to study them closely, drinking in their modelling and their perspective as dry earth drinks rain.

akbar-and-hawai.description: This is one page of a double-page scene from the illustrated history of Akbar's reign. In 1561 the 19-year-old emperor mounted the ferocious elephant Hawai and drove it after another elephant, across a bridge of boats on the Jumna at Agra. Beneath the two great beasts the boats sink and tilt like leaves under a storm's heel, and attendants leap into the water. Basawan designed the swirling composition, a whirlpool of bodies and river, and another artist laid in the colours.

battle-of-the-ascetics.description: Violence over a sacred thing is still violence, and a painting can hold both the fact and the craft without confusing them. In 1567 two rival bands of Hindu ascetics fought over the right to a sacred bathing place at Thanesar. Akbar watched, and let some of his soldiers join the fight. Basawan fills the page with dozens of near-naked, ash-smeared figures wielding swords and bows. Notice what he does with them: each body is shown in a different pose, with a vigour and anatomical study that were unmatched at the court. Here is the practice for you as a viewer: see the skill, and remember the fight was real. Admiration and gravity can share a single page.

vain-dervish.description: It comes from a small, exquisite manuscript of Jami's *Baharistan*, the "Spring Garden", made for Akbar's library in Lahore. Within it a proud dervish is taught humility by a wiser Sufi, as a high wave is taught by the shore. Basawan set the lesson in a soft, receding landscape, where the land fades into haze and a distant town waits like a memory, and in that fading he showed his mastery of atmospheric depth, learned partly from European models.

jain-ascetic.description: A lean Jain monk, robed in white, walked along a river beneath the trees, absorbed in thought, while life went on around him like water around a stone. This is a late, intimate work: an individual study of a holy man, not a page of history. In it lives the naturalism and the sympathy for ordinary people that Basawan passed on, as a lamp passes its flame, to the next generation of Mughal painters, among them his son Manohar.

boy-with-a-basket-of-fruit.description: It was painted soon after Caravaggio came to Rome, in the lean season when he sold pictures to survive. A young man, shoulder bare and lips parted, holds a basket overflowing with grapes, peaches and figs, an orchard gathered in his arms. So exact is the fruit that its species can be identified, as a naturalist names a bird by its feather. It is a sign of the young artist's commitment to painting straight from life.

medusa.description:
A real parade shield. A gift for the Grand Duke of Tuscany. And on it, the Gorgon's severed head. Screaming. Caught at the instant of death. Blood spurting. Snakes still writhing. The face is probably Caravaggio's own; he used himself as the model. The shield is convex. So the head does not stay put. It seems to jump forward, toward you.

It is still screaming.

judith-beheading-holofernes.description:
Judith, the Jewish heroine. Holofernes, the Assyrian general. She saws through his neck. Her face: determination. And disgust. Beside her, the old maid waits, eager, the sack ready. Behind them, nothing. A black background. A blood-red curtain. No distance anywhere. The violence is shockingly direct. The picture helped establish Caravaggio's reputation for brutal realism.

The sack is waiting.

calling-of-saint-matthew.description: This was Caravaggio's first public commission, and the painting that made him famous overnight, as a single spark wakes a whole field of dry grass. In a dim tax office, Christ enters from the right and points at Matthew, his hand an echo of God's hand in Michelangelo's *Creation of Adam*. A shaft of light cuts across the wall like a blade of dawn through a shuttered room, singling him out. Matthew sits among men in modern Roman dress and gestures as if to say, "Who, me?"

supper-at-emmaus.description: Two disciples had met a stranger on the road, and at the table the veil fell: he was the risen Christ. Recognition struck like lightning over still water. One pushes back his chair; the other flings his arms wide, and the gesture seems to break through the picture plane into our own space, as a wave breaks past the line of the shore. At the table's edge a basket of fruit teeters, and its shadow is painted with a realism that fools the eye.

entombment.description:
Christ's body. Lowered. Down toward a stone slab. The slab's sharp corner seems to push out at you, as if you stood inside the tomb. Then the mourners, falling in a diagonal. At the top, Mary Cleophas, arms thrown up. Lower. Lower. At the bottom, the dead man's hand, brushing the stone. Rubens made copies of it. Géricault, Cézanne and many others too.

The hand is still brushing the stone.

susanna-and-the-elders.description: Signed and dated when Artemisia was just 17, this is her earliest known painting. Two older men lean over a wall, bearing down on the bathing Susanna like a storm cloud over a lone tree, and she twists away in distress. Male painters had often treated the story as an excuse for an erotic nude. Artemisia turned the tale around and told it from Susanna's point of view: an experience of threat and violation, seen from within the one who bore it.

judith-slaying-holofernes.description:
Judith and her maid pin down the Assyrian general. They saw through his neck. Blood sprays in arcs across the white sheets. No hesitation here. Caravaggio's Judith was hesitant, delicate. Artemisia's women are strong. Working together. Physical effort. Many viewers read the painting in light of her own trial. But first of all it is a masterpiece of Baroque drama. An earlier version is in Naples.

Two versions. One scene.

self-portrait-as-saint-catherine.description: She gives her own features to the early Christian martyr, and I cannot stop looking at the face. She holds a palm. Beside her, the broken spiked wheel on which the saint was to be tortured. The painting dates from Artemisia's successful years in Florence. The National Gallery bought it in 2018, only the 21st painting by a woman to enter its collection. Only the 21st. I say it again to hear it. Then it toured Britain, including a GP surgery and a women's prison. Who gets to be seen, and where? Being seen is also a way of being counted.

jael-and-sisera.description:
Another Old Testament heroine. Jael. The hammer raised. The tent peg set to the temple of the sleeping enemy general, Sisera. He sleeps on. Her face is calm. Almost thoughtful. That is the worst of it: the calm, and the violence still to come. On the column at the right, Artemisia's signature. And the date.

The hammer has not fallen yet.

judith-and-her-maidservant.description:
After. The killing is done. A tent. A single candle. Judith raises her hand to shade the light. She listens. For danger. Sword still in hand. Her maid wraps the general's head in cloth. Suspense. Deep shadows. The glowing gold of Judith's dress. Together they make this one of the finest night scenes of the Caravaggesque movement.

She is still listening.

allegory-of-painting.description: She leans into the canvas with her brush raised, sleeves rolled up, a gold chain with a mask pendant at her neck, and I know that posture. I know the lean of work. I know the rolled sleeve. Artemisia shows herself as the personification of Painting itself. A male artist could paint the figure of Painting, but he could not become her. She claims both roles at once, the maker and the made. It was probably painted in London, where she joined her father at the court of Charles I. What would it mean to be both the subject and the hand? To make yourself is to be made twice.

old-woman-frying-eggs.description: An old woman cooks eggs in a clay dish while a boy brings a melon and a flask, and I am suddenly in a kitchen I have not stood in for years. Velázquez painted it in Seville when he was about 19: a *bodegón*, a kitchen scene with still life. I watch the eggs turning white in the oil. I watch the gleam on the brass mortar. I watch the shadows under a knife. All of it observed with astonishing precision for so young a painter. Who taught me to look this closely at the ordinary? Attention is the first form of love.

waterseller-of-seville.description: A dignified old water-seller hands a glass to a boy, solemn as a priest at an altar, while behind them a man drinks in the shadows. In the glass a fig floats to freshen the water, and on the great clay jug the drops bead like dew on stone at dawn. Velázquez gives a street vendor the gravity of a saint. Later the painting's own road turned strange: it was captured from Joseph Bonaparte's baggage after the Battle of Vitoria in 1813 and given to the Duke of Wellington.

surrender-of-breda.description: How you win says more about you than the winning. This canvas was painted for the Hall of Realms in the Buen Retiro Palace, and it commemorates a Spanish victory of 1625 in the war with the Dutch. Yet look at what Velázquez chose to show. Not triumph, but courtesy: the Spanish general Ambrogio Spinola lays a consoling hand on the shoulder of the defeated Justinus of Nassau as he hands over the city's keys. That hand is the whole doctrine of the picture. Behind the Spanish, a forest of upright lances gave the painting its popular name, *Las Lanzas*. The lances record the force; the hand records the grace. Victory is a ledger; courtesy is a covenant.

rokeby-venus.description: This is the only surviving female nude by Velázquez, a rare flower in the stern soil of Catholic Spain. Venus reclines with her back to us and gazes into a mirror held by Cupid, and there her face appears only as a soft blur, like a moon seen through mist. In 1914 the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed the canvas with a meat cleaver in protest at the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst. The wound was skilfully restored, and the goddess reclines still.

innocent-x.description: His gaze finds me before I find him: sharp, suspicious, fixed on the viewer, and today the viewer is me. Velázquez painted him during his second trip to Italy, the 75-year-old pope in shimmering red and white. Innocent is said to have remarked that it was *troppo vero*, "too true". I know that flinch. I have met my own likeness and looked away. Three centuries later it obsessed Francis Bacon, who painted dozens of screaming variations on it. What is it about being seen truly that makes us want to scream? The truest likeness is the one we cannot forgive.

las-meninas.description: The little Infanta Margarita stands at the heart of the room like a lamp in a dim hall, gathered about by her maids of honour, a dwarf, a dog and courtiers. At the left Velázquez himself stands at a vast canvas, brush poised, a watcher inside his own tale. On the back wall hangs a mirror, and in it appear the king and queen, standing, it seems, exactly where we stand, as though the glass had dissolved the threshold between their world and ours. Who is looking at whom? Its riddles of seeing and representation have made it perhaps the most analysed painting in Western art.

anatomy-lesson.description: This was Rembrandt's first big commission in Amsterdam, painted when he was 26. The city's leading anatomist demonstrates the muscles of a dissected arm, and seven surgeons lean in around him like reeds bent toward a single current, each face lit with its own kind of attention. Group portraits had usually been stiff rows of heads, set out like stones along a wall. Rembrandt turned this one into a dramatic scene of learning, and it made his name.

night-watch.description: A company of civic guardsmen bursts into motion as their captain gives the order to march, like a river breaking through a winter dam. Muskets are loaded, a drum beats, a dog barks, and among them a glowing girl carries the company's emblem, a chicken's claw, bright as a lantern in the throng. Yet this is no night scene. The name came from darkened varnish, dusk laid over a field of day, and later restorations removed it. Since 2019 the Rijksmuseum has studied and restored it in public, in a glass room.

hundred-guilder-print.description: Rembrandt's most ambitious print gathers several episodes from Matthew 19 around a radiant Christ, as a hearth gathers the cold: the sick being brought to him, mothers with children, arguing Pharisees and a rich young man. On the left the plate is densely worked, dark as a forest at dusk; on the right it is left almost bare, pale as morning. Its nickname comes from the very high price it was said to fetch.

self-portrait-with-two-circles.description: He stands before me with palette and brushes, in a plain fur-lined robe and a white cap, looking straight out, and I do not look away. This is one of the last and greatest of Rembrandt's roughly 80 self-portraits. The artist is ageing. He is bankrupt. He is still holding his brushes. Behind him, two mysterious arcs on the wall have been read as symbols of perfection, a map of the world, or a display of the painter's skill. I remember my own bad years. Which circle would I draw around my life? When the rest is gone, the looking remains.

jewish-bride.description: A couple stands in a tender embrace, probably portrayed as the biblical Isaac and Rebecca. His hand rests on her breast. Her hand touches his. I have known that gesture, the hand that answers a hand. The sleeves are built up with thick paint applied with a palette knife, glowing gold and red. Vincent van Gogh said he would give ten years of his life to sit in front of it for a fortnight with only a crust of bread. What would I give? Tenderness is the one thing paint cannot fake.

prodigal-son.description: The ragged son had come home at last. He kneels, shaven-headed and barefoot, and presses his face against his old father's chest, as a spent river presses into the sea. The father rests both hands on his back in forgiveness, and the light gathers there like warmth in a hearth. From the right the elder brother watches, cold as a winter stone. It was painted near the end of Rembrandt's life, and it is one of the most moving images of mercy in art.

st-pauls-cathedral.description: What you see is rarely what holds you up. This is Wren's masterpiece, the building he spent 35 years on, rising on the site of a medieval cathedral gutted in the Great Fire of London. Consider its dome, which is really three shells in one. A shallow inner dome, seen from the floor. A hidden brick cone that carries the real structural load. A tall outer dome of timber and lead that gives St Paul's its skyline silhouette. Said plainly: the beauty you admire and the strength that bears the weight are different layers of one architecture. Wren's son laid the final stone in 1710. A life's work can be finished by another's hand.

royal-observatory-greenwich.description: Orientation is a decision before it is a discovery. This observatory was built in under a year for the newly created post of Astronomer Royal, held by John Flamsteed, on the foundations of an old fort in Greenwich Park. Wren, himself a former professor of astronomy, oriented the main hall along a north-south meridian. Notice the order of things: first a line drawn for a building, later a line the world would measure by. The site later gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time and to the line of zero longitude. Where you choose to stand can become the place others begin.

royal-hospital-chelsea.description: Dignity is an architecture, not an ornament. This is a retirement and nursing home for army veterans, commissioned by Charles II and modelled loosely on Les Invalides in Paris. Look at how it is arranged: around three plain, dignified brick courtyards rather than a single showpiece facade. You can read that plan as a sentence in brick: the life inside counts for more than the face turned outward. It still houses several hundred retired soldiers, known as Chelsea Pensioners, who continue to wear the scarlet coats introduced in Wren's time. A lineage can be worn. Care that lasts is built for living in, not for looking at.

st-stephen-walbrook.description: Every great work has a rehearsal somewhere nearby. This is one of more than fifty City parish churches Wren rebuilt after the Great Fire. It was squeezed onto an awkward, irregular plot, and yet it is crowned with a coffered dome carried on slender Corinthian columns. That dome is widely read as his working study for the dome of St Paul's, then still on the drawing board a few streets away. Think of it as a sketch you can stand inside. The practice: try the hard thing small before you try it large. Constraint is the first draft of grace.

monument-to-the-great-fire.description: A memorial can be a measurement. This fluted Doric column was raised, with Robert Hooke, near the bakery where the Great Fire of 1666 began. Its height of 202 feet is equal to its exact distance from the fire's starting point. Read that plainly: the monument is a ruler laid down between the disaster and its remembrance. A gilded urn of flames tops the column. Inside, 311 steps of a spiral staircase lead to a viewing platform still open to the public. You climb the memory on your own legs. Some ledgers are kept in stone and paid in steps.

the-milkmaid.description: She pours a thin stream of milk into an earthenware bowl, utterly absorbed in her work, and I hold my breath so as not to disturb her. A sturdy kitchen maid. A window. A light. The light picks out the crusty bread in dots of paint. It finds the nail holes in the plaster wall. It finds the ultramarine of her apron. I remember hands like hers at work like this. Vermeer makes a simple household task feel timeless and quietly heroic. The smallest labour, done wholly, is a kind of prayer.

the-little-street.description: Here stand ordinary brick houses in Delft, weathered as old riverbanks. A woman sews in a doorway, another is busy in an alleyway, and children play on the pavement like sparrows in the dust. Every crack and patch of whitewash is lovingly recorded, as memory keeps the lines of a beloved face. In 2015 archival research identified the exact site, on the Vlamingstraat, where Vermeer's aunt lived.

view-of-delft.description: Across the water lay Vermeer's hometown on a morning after rain, beneath clouds that towered like the ramparts of a second city in the sky. Parts of the town lay drowned in shadow while sunlight struck a distant church tower and the rooftops, as a torch finds gold in a dark hall. He mixed sand into some of his paint to catch the texture of brick and stone, so that the walls hold grit as well as light. In Proust's *In Search of Lost Time*, the writer Bergotte dies gazing at its "little patch of yellow wall".

woman-holding-a-balance.description: She holds a small balance up to the soft window light, and the pans are empty. I notice that first: empty. A woman in a fur-trimmed jacket, at a table strewn with pearls and gold, weighing nothing at all. Behind her, on the wall, hangs a painting of the Last Judgment, when souls are weighed. I think of what I would put on the scale. I think of what I have kept. The picture is a meditation on balance, temperance and the choices of daily life. Every day is a small judgment we hold up to the light.

the-art-of-painting.description: A heavy tapestry is drawn back like a curtain of evening, and behind it a painter, seen from behind, paints a model dressed as Clio, the muse of history, with a trumpet and a book. A large map of the Netherlands covers the back wall, a land spread out like a sleeper. Vermeer kept this allegory of his art until his death. Its later road ran through darkness: in 1940 it was bought by Adolf Hitler; after the war it went to Vienna, and restitution claims for it were rejected in 2011.

geumgang-jeondo.description: Here the famous Diamond Mountains of Korea's east coast are seen as if from the air, gathered into a great circular composition like a world held in a cupped palm. Sharp white granite peaks, drawn in vertical, needle-like strokes, rise like spears of frost around softer, wooded earthen hills rendered with wet dots. Jeong Seon balanced them like the yin and yang of Korean thought, stone and soil, hard and yielding. It is one of the landmark images of Korean art.

cheongpunggye.description: At the foot of Mount Inwang in Seoul lay a wooded valley, and there a scholarly family kept a pavilion among pines and rocks, sheltered as a nest in the crook of a branch. Jeong Seon painted many such views of real places in and around the capital. Here he mixed dense, dark ink with lighter washes, shadow and mist woven together, to catch the texture of the hills he knew from daily walks, hills worn into memory as a path is worn into grass.

pungak-naesan-chongram.description: Here is another vision of the Diamond Mountains, this time in autumn, when they are called Pungak, "maple mountain", as though the season itself had renamed them. Temples and hermitages are tucked among the crowded peaks like pearls caught in folds of stone, and touches of red foliage glow among them like embers. Jeong Seon travelled to Mount Geumgang several times from 1711, and he painted it throughout his life, returning to it as a river returns to the sea.

bakyeon-falls.description: Near Kaesong a waterfall, counted among the "three wonders" of that old capital, crashes down a sheer cliff into a deep pool like a white dragon diving for the dark. Far below, tiny visitors watch. Jeong Seon exaggerated the height of the falls and darkened the cliffs with heavy ink, so that the white water seems to roar out of the picture as thunder rolls out of a gorge.

inwang-jesaekdo.description: This is Jeong Seon's masterpiece, painted when he was 75. The granite peaks of Mount Inwang, behind the royal palace in Seoul, rise dark and wet after a summer rain, gleaming like the flanks of a great beast new from the river, while mist drifts through the pine woods below. The rock faces are built with broad, heavy sweeps of ink, a daring technique for its time. According to tradition, he painted it hoping for the recovery of his dying friend, the poet Yi Byeong-yeon, as if clearing skies could be wished upon a failing life. It entered the national collection in 2021 as part of the Lee Kun-hee donation.

cat-on-an-autumn-day.description: Not all of Jeong Seon's work is grand landscape; not every song he sang was of mountains. Here a cat sits among autumn flowers, alert and relaxed at once, like a calm pond that holds the whole sky. Small paintings of animals, insects and plants were popular with Korean collectors. This one shows his gentle observation of everyday nature, the eye that measured peaks now resting on a single cat.

nude-maja.description: A young woman reclines on green cushions, arms behind her head, and looks straight at the viewer, needing neither shame nor a myth to hide behind, plain as daylight on water. It is one of the earliest Western paintings of a real nude woman who is not a goddess. It was probably made for the royal favourite Manuel Godoy, who also owned its clothed pendant, *La maja vestida*, the pair like day and its shadow. In 1815 the Inquisition summoned Goya to explain the "obscene" picture.

sleep-of-reason.description:
A man at a desk. Asleep. Slumped. Perhaps Goya himself. Behind him the darkness moves. Owls. Bats. A lynx, staring. They swarm out of the dark and he does not wake. The title is inscribed on the desk. It comes from *Los Caprichos*, 80 satirical prints attacking superstition, ignorance and the abuses of Spanish society. The image has become an emblem of the Enlightenment. And of its fears.

The darkness behind him is still full.

family-of-charles-iv.description: They stand in a row in glittering silks and sashes, the Spanish royal family, and I look for the one who is not glittering. The queen, Maria Luisa, dominates the centre. The king looks vacant. The honesty of it has sometimes been read as satire, and I wonder when honesty began to look like mockery. Then I find him: in a nod to Velázquez's *Las Meninas*, Goya painted himself in the shadows at the left, working at a large canvas. I know that place. I have stood at the edge of rooms not quite mine. Sometimes the truest witness is the one in the dark.

second-of-may.description: Some paintings refuse to give you a hero, and that refusal is the lesson. The people of Madrid rise up against Napoleon's troops, attacking the Egyptian Mameluke cavalry with knives in a tangle of horses, bodies and blood. It was painted after the French were expelled, yet it shows no heroes, only the chaos and fury of street fighting. Hold that plainly: war seen up close has no centre to stand in. Memory owes the dead the truth of the tangle.

hokusai-manga.description: A teacher's notebook can outgrow the classroom. Here are fifteen volumes of sketches, published from 1814 onwards, the last appearing long after Hokusai's death. They show thousands of subjects: people at work and play, animals, plants, gods, ghosts, landscapes and comic figures, all drawn with wit and economy. Think of it as a grammar of seeing, set down one line at a time. It was meant as a model book for students, and the *Manga* became a best-seller. It was also one of the first Japanese books to excite European artists in the 1850s–60s. Make a thing to teach, and it may teach far beyond your reach.

fine-wind-clear-morning.description: Mount Fuji rises alone, turned red by early morning light in late summer, like an ember set against a blue sky, and that sky is filled with rows of mackerel clouds, scaled like a great fish swimming overhead.
